evidence: Cic. Rosc. Com. 42: is jam prīdem mortuus est (Lewis & Short s.v. jamprīdem)
terms.comment: With a past tense it says that something happened long ago; with a present, that it has been so for a long time (see already). “Ago” with a number is abhinc: abhinc decem annōs.

evidence: Hor. S. 2.2.46: haud ita prīdem (Lewis & Short s.v. prīdem)
Cic. Brut. 41: nostrā cīvitāte nōn ita prīdem dominātū rēgiō līberātā (Lewis & Short)

terms.gloss: a while ago, just now, earlier
terms.register: vōx sermōnis cotīdiānī: Plaut., Ter.; Cic. in epistulīs
evidence: Plaut. Amph. 2.2.59: Dūdum? Quam dūdum istuc factum est? (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: A shorter time than prīdem: earlier today, a little while ago. Lewis & Short note that outside comedy, Cicero's letters and philosophical works and Vergil it is rare except in jam dūdum.

terms.gloss: long since, a long time ago; for a long time now
evidence: Ter. Eun. 738: ego jamdūdum hīc adsum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Often “for a good while now”, of something still going on.

sources: Lewis & Short: jampridem · Lewis & Short: pridem · Lewis & Short: dudum
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 86, 89, each phrase checked against the searchable text of the book.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
